project.objective: Determine the true birthplace of Elizabeth Mariah (Turnbow) Barker (b. ~1823), wife of Jonathan Barker, and explain why the 1850 census index says England while the 1860-1880 censuses say Alabama.
project.title: Elizabeth Turnbow Barker's birthplace

researcher_profile.narration_guidance: One-line preamble per skill invocation explaining what you're about to do. Assume basic GPS vocabulary. Define unusual or specialized terminology inline.

exhaustive_declaration.justification: Every federal census in which Elizabeth appears (1850 original image plus index, 1860, 1870, 1880) was examined, and so were her daughters' censuses that give a mother's birthplace (Sarah Martha 1880; Amanda 1880 original, 1900, 1910). A FAN survey covered the 1850 Turnbow households, and the church record attached in the tree, the Mississippi death-certificate index and the Find a Grave index were checked. Alabama did not require birth registration until 1908, so the census testimony is the main evidence that exists for a woman born in 1823. The question is answered at state level (Alabama). The county is not named in any record and would need a separate question.

stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: c_001 is resolved in favor of Alabama. England is explained as a derivative transcription error, and Mississippi as a daughter's second-hand answer.
stop_criteria.evidence_class: Original 1850 schedule (src_001), with the information likely supplied by Elizabeth or her husband. It is direct evidence of birthplace, with informant quality indeterminate.
stop_criteria.goal_alignment: Yes. Five records, including the original 1850 page, give Alabama, and the England reading is shown to be an indexing line-shift.
stop_criteria.independent_verification: Four separate enumerations of her own household (1850-1880) plus her daughter Sarah Martha in a separate household. These share a family informant pool but are distinct recordings by different enumerators.
stop_criteria.original_substitution: The decisive 1850 entry and the 1880 Ainsworth line were verified on original images. The 1860, 1870 and 1880 Barker entries remain index-only but are consistent with each other.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: Low for the state. An obituary, a Bible record or a true LDS membership register could name a county, but none is likely to move her birth out of Alabama given five concordant statements and the Turnbow siblings' Alabama births.
stop_criteria.repository_breadth: Federal censuses 1850-1910, the Mississippi death-certificate index, Find a Grave index, the LDS district minutes and Turnbow FAN censuses were searched on FamilySearch. No vital birth records exist for Alabama in 1823.

questions.question: Where was Elizabeth Mariah Barker (wife of Jonathan Barker of Jasper and Smith counties, Mississippi, born about 1823) born — England, as the 1850 census index states, or Alabama, as the 1860–1880 censuses and the FamilySearch tree state?
questions.rationale: The 1850 U.S. census index gives her birthplace as England while three later censuses give Alabama; the conflict must be resolved before her parentage can be researched, because the place of birth determines which Turnbow family (if any) she belongs to. Records with direct birthplace statements (four federal censuses, an 1883–85 LDS Mississippi Conference membership record attached in the tree, and her daughters' later records naming a mother's birthplace) are available and searchable.

conflicts.description: Elizabeth (Turnbow) Barker's birthplace: England (1850 census index), Alabama (1850 original schedule; 1860, 1870, 1880 censuses; daughter Sarah Martha 1880), or Mississippi (daughter Amanda's 1880, 1900, 1910 censuses).
conflicts.independence_analysis: a_005 is not independent of a_001: it is FamilySearch's index of the very same 1850 page, so the two are one evidence unit and the original (a_001) controls. a_001, a_006, a_007 and a_008 are four separate enumerations (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) in two counties by different enumerators; the informant each time was a member of Elizabeth's own household, very likely Elizabeth herself or Jonathan. They are independent recordings but share an informant pool, so they show a consistent family answer rather than four unrelated witnesses. a_011 (Sarah Martha, 1880) comes from a separate household, but she lived next door and could have learned it from her mother at any time, so it is only partly independent of Elizabeth's own answer. a_013, a_015 and a_016 come from a third household (Amanda Ainsworth, Smith Co.) with one daughter or son-in-law as informant across three censuses; they are one evidence unit repeated, and a_015 is already compromised because the same line gives Amanda's English father a Mississippi birthplace.
conflicts.resolution_rationale: The problem: Elizabeth Barker's birthplace is recorded as England, Alabama, and Mississippi, and the answer decides where to look for her birth family. The evidence: the 1850 Jasper County census, as indexed online, says England. But the handwritten 1850 page itself reads 'England' on her husband Jonathan's line and 'Alabama' on hers. The censuses of 1860, 1870 and 1880, all answered by someone in her own home, say Alabama; so does her daughter Sarah Martha, living next door in 1880. Her daughter Amanda, in another county, said in 1880 and 1910 that her mother was born in Mississippi (and in 1900 gave Mississippi for both parents, although her father was English). Which is more reliable: Elizabeth's own household, repeated four times and confirmed on the original 1850 page, is the strongest and most consistent testimony. The England entry is not testimony at all but a copying error, and Amanda's answers are second-hand and partly wrong on their face. Alabama is preferred (a_001). Why the other answers exist: the England reading is a derivative transcription error — the modern indexer slid the birthplace column down one line, giving Elizabeth her husband's 'England' and each child the next person's place. The Mississippi answers fit the familiar pattern of a child reporting a parent's birthplace from family memory: Amanda grew up in Mississippi among Turnbow relatives settled there since about 1830, and the family's earlier home in Madison County was part of the Mississippi Territory until 1817, so 'Mississippi' was an easy, plausible-sounding answer for someone who never saw the place.
conflicts.weighing_analysis: Decisive factors: (1) Format — the England reading exists only in the derivative index; the original 1850 schedule (a_001) says Alabama for Elizabeth and puts England on Jonathan's line. An index cannot outweigh the page it was copied from. (2) Informant proximity — the Alabama answers come from Elizabeth's own household four times over 30 years; she is the person best placed to know where she was told she was born. The Mississippi answers come from a daughter (or her husband) reporting a parent's birthplace, which is hearsay by definition. (3) Consistency and plausibility — Alabama is given in 1850 (original), 1860, 1870 and 1880 and by Sarah Martha; it fits a family whose candidate parents married in Madison Co., Mississippi Territory (now Alabama) in 1816 and whose candidate siblings John (b.~1817) and Joseph (b.~1819) Turnbow both report Alabama births, with the Turnbows recorded in Mississippi only from c.1830. Amanda's answers are internally weak (1900 also gives her English-born father a Mississippi birthplace).

proof_summaries.exhaustive_search_summary: Searched all four federal censuses in which Elizabeth appears (1850 Jasper Co., with the original image examined; 1860 and 1870 Smith Co.; 1880 Raleigh, Smith Co.). Also searched her daughters' censuses that report a mother's birthplace (Sarah Martha Lovett 1880; Amanda Ainsworth 1880 [original line checked], 1900, 1910), the 1850 Turnbow households in Mississippi (FAN), the Mississippi Death Certificate Index 1912-1943 (daughters not found), the Find a Grave index (no memorial found), and the LDS Mississippi District minutes attached in the tree (no mention). Not searched: original images of the 1860/1870/1880 Barker entries, a true LDS record-of-members register, newspapers, Confederate pension files, and any Alabama county source naming a birth county. Alabama did not require birth registration until 1908.
proof_summaries.narrative_markdown:
# Birthplace of Elizabeth Mariah (Turnbow) Barker (c. 1823)

**Conclusion (Probable):** Elizabeth, wife of the English-born blacksmith and farmer Jonathan Barker of Jasper and Smith counties, Mississippi, was born about 1823 in **Alabama**, not England. The FamilySearch tree records her as Elizabeth Mariah Turnbow (KWJ6-RPH). The "England" birthplace attached to her comes from an indexing error.

## The problem

The online index to the 1850 U.S. census for Jasper County, Mississippi, gives Elizabeth Barker's birthplace as England.[1] Later records give Alabama, and one daughter said Mississippi. Her birthplace decides where to look for her birth family.

## The evidence

**1850 — the original page.** On the handwritten 1850 schedule, the Barker household reads: Jonathan Barker, 30, blacksmith, born *England*; Elizabeth, 27, born *Alabama*; Sarah Martha, 4, born *Mississippi*; Amanda P., 2.[2] The informant is not named; in practice it was usually the wife or husband. This is an original record.

**Her own household, 1860-1880.** Every later census of the household gives Alabama for Elizabeth: 1860 Smith County (about age 36),[3] 1870 Smith County (about 47),[4] and 1880 Raleigh, Smith County (56, wife of "John" Barker, born England).[5] Each was taken by a different enumerator. All of these answers come from Elizabeth's own household, so they show one consistent family answer over thirty years.

**Her daughters.** In 1880, daughter Martha S. (Sarah Martha) Lovett lived next door to the Barkers. She gave her father's birthplace as England and her mother's as **Alabama**.[5] Daughter Amanda Ainsworth, in another part of Smith County, gave her mother's birthplace as **Mississippi** in 1880 and 1910.[6][8] In 1900 she gave Mississippi for both parents, although her father was English.[7]

**The Turnbow family (context).** The tree names her parents as Robert F. Turnbow and Sarah Canterberry, married in September 1816 in Madison County, Mississippi Territory, an area that became part of Alabama in 1817. No record found here states that they were Elizabeth's parents. This is context only and is not used to prove the birthplace.

## Resolving the conflict

*England* is not testimony at all. It exists only in the modern index, and on the original page it sits on Jonathan's line. The indexer moved the birthplace column down one row: Elizabeth received her husband's "England," Sarah Martha received Elizabeth's "Alabama," and Amanda received Sarah Martha's "Mississippi."[1][2]

*Mississippi* is a second-hand answer from one daughter, repeated across three censuses with the same informant. One of those entries is plainly wrong about her father. Amanda grew up in Mississippi among relatives settled there since about 1830, and the family's earlier home in Madison County had been part of the Mississippi Territory. A child reporting a parent's birthplace from family memory could easily give that answer.

*Alabama* comes from the original 1850 page and three later censuses of Elizabeth's own household. Her next-door daughter gave the same answer.

## Limits

The tier is **probable**, not proved. Only the 1850 entry has been examined in the original. The 1860-1880 Barker entries were read from indexes. No record names the informant, and no record gives a county of birth. A county could come from an obituary, a Bible record, the original LDS record-of-members register for the Mississippi Conference, or the original 1860-1880 census pages. This conclusion does not establish her parentage, which needs its own research question.

## Sources

2. 1850 U.S. census, Jasper Co., Mississippi, population schedule, image 73 of 104, Jonathan Barker household; FamilySearch image ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-DC1S-623.
3. "United States, Census, 1860," FamilySearch, Elizabeth Barker in household of Jonathan Barker, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:M6GV-MGR).
4. "United States, Census, 1870," FamilySearch, Elizabeth Barker, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:MFSR-DYF).
5. "United States, Census, 1880," FamilySearch, Raleigh, Smith, Mississippi, sheet 295C-D, John and Elisabeth Barker and Major W. and Martha S. Lovett households (ark:/61903/3:1:33S7-9YB8-HDX).
6. 1880 U.S. census, Smith Co., Mississippi, Beat 2, ED 104, sheet 310C, Asbery Ainsworth household; FamilySearch image ark:/61903/3:1:33SQ-GYB8-WKM.
